## The test

**Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference.** If bundle $x^{1}$ was chosen when $x^{2}$ was affordable, then $x^{2}$ must **never** be chosen when $x^{1}$ is affordable.

A utility maximiser cannot violate this: if they picked $x^{1}$ over an affordable $x^{2}$, then $x^{1}\succsim x^{2}$, and that ranking cannot reverse.

## The data

| | prices | chosen bundle |
|---|---|---|
| Observation 1 | $p^{1}=(2,4)$ | $x^{1}=(1,2)$ |
| Observation 2 | $p^{2}=(6,3)$ | $x^{2}=(2,1)$ |

## Step 1 — At the first price vector

$$p^{1}\!\cdot x^{1}=2(1)+4(2)=\mathbf{10} \qquad\qquad p^{1}\!\cdot x^{2}=2(2)+4(1)=\mathbf{8}$$

The consumer spent 10 and chose $x^{1}$. The bundle $x^{2}$ would have cost only 8 — comfortably **affordable**, and they did not take it.

$$\Longrightarrow\quad x^{1}\ \text{is revealed preferred to}\ x^{2}$$

## Step 2 — At the second price vector

$$p^{2}\!\cdot x^{2}=6(2)+3(1)=\mathbf{15} \qquad\qquad p^{2}\!\cdot x^{1}=6(1)+3(2)=\mathbf{12}$$

Now they spent 15 and chose $x^{2}$, while $x^{1}$ would have cost only 12 — again **affordable**, again rejected.

$$\Longrightarrow\quad x^{2}\ \text{is revealed preferred to}\ x^{1}$$

## Verdict

$$x^{1}\succ x^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad x^{2}\succ x^{1}$$

Both directions hold, which is a direct contradiction. **WARP is violated, so this consumer is not maximising a well-behaved utility function.**

Note how little the argument needed: no utility function, no indifference curves, no differentiability — just four multiplications and two comparisons. That is the power of revealed preference as a *test*.

## What the result does and does not establish

**It does** rule out utility maximisation over a stable preference ordering. No such ordering can rank each bundle strictly above the other.

**It does not** prove the consumer is irrational in any everyday sense. The inconsistency is equally well explained by something the model holds fixed having changed — tastes shifting between the observations, a different context, or a good being mismeasured. The question's phrase *"nothing else of significance changed"* is doing essential work: it is precisely that assumption which converts an observed inconsistency into a verdict about maximisation.

**The general lesson.** WARP is a **necessary** condition. Passing it does not prove utility maximisation — for three or more observations you also need the chains to be free of cycles, which is SARP — but failing it is decisive, and this consumer fails it.

> **The three results.**
> $$x(p,w)=\left(\frac{ap}{w}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-a}},\qquad y(p,w)=\left(\frac{ap}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}$$
> $$\pi(p,w)=(1-a)\,p^{\frac{1}{1-a}}\left(\frac{a}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}$$

## Step 1 — The problem

The firm chooses the input $x$ to maximise revenue minus cost:

$$\max_{x\ge0}\;\pi=p\,f(x)-w\,x=p\,x^{a}-w\,x$$

$p$ is the output price, $w$ the factor price. Both are taken as given — this is a **competitive** firm, and saying so justifies treating $p$ as a constant when differentiating.

## Step 2 — First-order condition

$$\frac{d\pi}{dx}=p\,a\,x^{a-1}-w=0$$

$$\Longrightarrow\quad \underbrace{p\cdot MP_x}_{\text{marginal revenue product}}=\underbrace{w}_{\text{marginal cost of the input}}$$

**State the economics.** Hire the input up to the point where the value of what the last unit produces exactly equals what it costs. Below that point an extra unit adds more revenue than cost; beyond it, less.

## Step 3 — Factor demand function

Solve the FOC for $x$:

$$p\,a\,x^{a-1}=w\;\Longrightarrow\;x^{a-1}=\frac{w}{ap}\;\Longrightarrow\;x^{1-a}=\frac{ap}{w}$$

$$\boxed{\;x(p,w)=\left(\frac{ap}{w}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-a}}\;}$$

**Read it off.** Factor demand is **decreasing in $w$** and **increasing in $p$** — both as expected. It depends on $p$ and $w$ only through the ratio $p/w$, which is why it is homogeneous of degree zero in prices: doubling both leaves the firm's real problem unchanged.

## Step 4 — Output supply function

Substitute the optimal input back into the technology:

$$y(p,w)=\big[x(p,w)\big]^{a}=\left(\frac{ap}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}$$

$$\boxed{\;y(p,w)=\left(\frac{ap}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}\;}$$

Upward-sloping in $p$, as any competitive supply curve must be.

## Step 5 — Profit function

Substitute both into $\pi=py-wx$. Write $A=(ap/w)^{\frac{1}{1-a}}$ so that $x=A$ and $y=A^{a}$:

$$\pi=p\,A^{a}-w\,A=A^{a}\left(p-wA^{1-a}\right)$$

But $A^{1-a}=ap/w$ by construction, so $wA^{1-a}=ap$ and the bracket collapses:

$$\pi=A^{a}\,(p-ap)=(1-a)\,p\,A^{a}$$

$$\boxed{\;\pi(p,w)=(1-a)\,p\left(\frac{ap}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}=(1-a)\,p^{\frac{1}{1-a}}\left(\frac{a}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}\;}$$

## Step 6 — The conditions that make this valid

**Second-order condition.** For the FOC to identify a maximum we need

$$\frac{d^{2}\pi}{dx^{2}}=p\,a(a-1)x^{a-2}<0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a<1$$

So the derivation requires **$0<a<1$**: decreasing returns to scale.

**Why that restriction is not a technicality.** If $a>1$ the technology has increasing returns; profit rises without bound and **no profit-maximising plan exists**. If $a=1$ the firm makes either zero profit (when $p=w$) or unbounded profit — the supply correspondence is not single-valued. The interior solution above exists *only* under decreasing returns, and the factor $(1-a)$ sitting in front of the profit function is the visible trace of that.

**Verification by Hotelling's lemma.** The profit function must satisfy

$$\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial p}=y(p,w),\qquad -\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial w}=x(p,w)$$

Differentiating our $\pi$ with respect to $p$ returns exactly $(ap/w)^{a/(1-a)}$, which is $y$. The answer checks out, and showing the check is worth doing.

## Statement of WAPM

Suppose we observe a firm choosing the net output vector $y^{t}$ when facing prices $p^{t}$, and $y^{s}$ when facing $p^{s}$. If the firm is maximising profit over an unchanging technology, then each observed choice must have been at least as profitable as the other one *at the prices actually ruling*:

$$\boxed{\;p^{t}y^{t}\ge p^{t}y^{s}\qquad\text{and}\qquad p^{s}y^{s}\ge p^{s}y^{t}\;}$$

**In words.** At period-$t$ prices the firm could have chosen $y^{s}$ — it was technologically available — and it did not. So $y^{t}$ must have been worth at least as much. The same reasoning runs the other way at period-$s$ prices.

Note that $y$ is a vector of **net** outputs: outputs positive, inputs negative. That convention is what lets a single inner product $p\cdot y$ stand for revenue minus cost.

## Deriving $\Delta p\,\Delta y\ge0$

**Step 1 — Rewrite both inequalities with everything on one side.**

$$p^{t}y^{t}-p^{t}y^{s}\ge0$$
$$p^{s}y^{s}-p^{s}y^{t}\ge0$$

**Step 2 — Add them.** The sum of two nonnegative numbers is nonnegative:

$$p^{t}y^{t}-p^{t}y^{s}+p^{s}y^{s}-p^{s}y^{t}\ge0$$

**Step 3 — Factor.** Group the $p^{t}$ terms and the $p^{s}$ terms:

$$p^{t}\left(y^{t}-y^{s}\right)-p^{s}\left(y^{t}-y^{s}\right)\ge0$$

$$\left(p^{t}-p^{s}\right)\left(y^{t}-y^{s}\right)\ge0$$

**Step 4 — Write it compactly.** With $\Delta p=p^{t}-p^{s}$ and $\Delta y=y^{t}-y^{s}$:

$$\boxed{\;\Delta p\,\Delta y\ge0\;}$$

The inner product of the price-change vector with the associated net-output change is nonnegative.

## What the inequality tells us

This single result contains **all** the comparative-statics predictions of profit maximisation. Take one price at a time, holding the others fixed, so the inner product reduces to one term:

- **Output supply slopes upward.** If only the output price changes, $\Delta p_{y}\Delta y\ge0$: price and quantity move together.
- **Factor demand slopes downward.** For an input, net output is *negative*, $y_i=-x_i$. So $\Delta w_i\,\Delta(-x_i)\ge0$, which is $\Delta w_i\,\Delta x_i\le0$: a higher factor price never raises the quantity of that factor used.

Both come from the *axiom alone* — no differentiability, no convexity, no functional form. That robustness is the point of the revealed-preference approach.

## Recoverability — reconstructing the technology

We never observe the production set $Y$; we observe choices. WAPM bounds $Y$ from outside.

Every observed choice was feasible, so $y^{1},\dots,y^{T}\in Y$. And if the firm chose $y^{t}$ at prices $p^{t}$, any plan $y$ with $p^{t}y>p^{t}y^{t}$ cannot have been available — it would have been taken. Each observation therefore cuts away a half-space, leaving

$$\hat{Y}=\left\{\,y\;:\;p^{t}y\le p^{t}y^{t}\ \text{ for all } t=1,\dots,T\,\right\}$$

$\hat Y$ is the smallest set consistent with the data, $Y\subseteq\hat Y$, and every new observation shrinks it.

**State the limit.** Because each observation is a supporting hyperplane, this recovers only the **convex, monotonic hull** of the true technology. A price-taking firm is never observed choosing a point in a "dent", so no amount of data can reveal a non-convexity.

**Conclusion.** WAPM is the firm-side analogue of WARP: a testable restriction on data, the standard comparative statics without calculus, and a bound on the unobservable technology — up to convexification.

## Setting up

$$\max_{x\ge0}\;\pi=p\,x^{a}-w\,x,\qquad 0<a<1$$

The restriction $a<1$ gives decreasing returns, which is what makes an interior maximum exist at all.

## Step 1 — Factor demand

$$\frac{d\pi}{dx}=p\,a\,x^{a-1}-w=0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x^{a-1}=\frac{w}{ap}$$

Raise both sides to the power $1/(a-1)$, remembering that $a-1<0$ so the inequality direction of the exponent flips the fraction:

$$\boxed{\;x(p,w)=\left(\frac{a\,p}{w}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-a}}\;}$$

**Check the second-order condition:** $d^{2}\pi/dx^{2}=p\,a(a-1)x^{a-2}<0$ since $a<1$. A maximum, as required.

## Step 2 — Output supply

$$y(p,w)=x^{a}=\left(\frac{a\,p}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}$$

## Step 3 — The profit function

$$\pi=p\,y-w\,x =p\left(\frac{ap}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}-w\left(\frac{ap}{w}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-a}}$$

Factor out the common term $\left(\frac{ap}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}$ and simplify:

$$\boxed{\;\pi(p,w)=(1-a)\;p^{\frac{1}{1-a}}\left(\frac{a}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}\;}$$

## Step 4 — Verifying homogeneity of degree one

Replace $p$ by $tp$ and $w$ by $tw$:

$$\pi(tp,tw)=(1-a)\,(tp)^{\frac{1}{1-a}}\left(\frac{a}{tw}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}} =(1-a)\,t^{\frac{1}{1-a}}p^{\frac{1}{1-a}}\cdot t^{-\frac{a}{1-a}}\left(\frac{a}{w}\right)^{\frac{a}{1-a}}$$

Collect the powers of $t$:

$$t^{\frac{1}{1-a}-\frac{a}{1-a}}=t^{\frac{1-a}{1-a}}=t^{1}$$

Hence

$$\pi(tp,tw)=t\,\pi(p,w)\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Numerical check.** With $a=\tfrac12$, $p=3$, $w=2$: $\pi=1.125$. Scaling both prices by $t=5$ gives $\pi(15,10)=5.625=5\times1.125$. ✓

## What homogeneity means

Doubling *every* price — the output price and the input price together — doubles profit but changes **nothing real**. Note that $x(p,w)$ and $y(p,w)$ are homogeneous of degree **zero**: the firm makes exactly the same physical plan.

This is the firm-side counterpart of the consumer's no-money-illusion property. Only **relative** prices drive behaviour; the absolute price level is a pure unit of account. A general inflation that lifts all prices proportionally leaves the firm's real decision untouched and simply rescales the money value of its profit.

## (A) Economic profit is not accounting profit

Both subtract cost from revenue. They disagree about **what counts as a cost**.

**Accounting profit** subtracts only *explicit* costs — money actually paid out: wages, materials, rent, interest.

**Economic profit** subtracts explicit costs **and** *implicit* costs: the value of resources the firm owns and uses, measured at their **opportunity cost** — what they would have earned in their best alternative use.

$$\text{Economic profit}=\text{Revenue}-\text{Explicit costs}-\text{Implicit costs}$$

**The items accountants leave out** are the owner's own labour, the capital they have tied up, and premises they own rather than rent. None involves a payment, so none appears in the accounts — but each has a foregone alternative.

**A worked example.** Someone leaves a job paying 8 lakh a year and invests 20 lakh of savings, which would have earned 2 lakh in interest. The business takes 30 lakh in revenue and pays 20 lakh in explicit costs.

$$\text{Accounting profit}=30-20=10\ \text{lakh}$$
$$\text{Economic profit}=30-20-\underbrace{8}_{\text{forgone salary}}-\underbrace{2}_{\text{forgone interest}}=0$$

The accounts show a healthy business; economically the owner is **exactly indifferent** between running it and taking the job back. That is why economics uses this measure — **zero economic profit means resources are earning what they could earn elsewhere**, and is the long-run competitive equilibrium condition. Zero accounting profit would mean the firm is failing.

## (B) The two constraints

A firm maximising $\pi=p\,f(x)-w\cdot x$ is not free to choose whatever it likes. Two things bind.

**1. The technological constraint.** The firm can only choose production plans that are actually **feasible** — plans lying in the production set $Y$, equivalently satisfying $y\le f(x)$.

This is the constraint that makes the problem interesting. Without it the firm would produce infinite output from no inputs. It is why diminishing marginal product matters, and why the second-order condition $f''\le0$ is needed for a maximum to exist at all — under increasing returns no profit-maximising plan exists.

**2. The market constraint.** The firm must take the **prices it faces** as given.

For a **competitive** firm this is the strong version: it is a price taker in both output and input markets, so $p$ and $w$ are constants and it can sell any quantity at $p$. This is what licenses treating prices as fixed when differentiating, and it is the assumption behind the first-order condition $p\,f'(x^{*})=w$.

A firm with market power faces a downward-sloping demand curve $p(y)$ instead, and its condition becomes $MR=MC$ with $MR<p$ — a different and more restrictive market constraint.

> **The distinction to state:** the technological constraint says what is **possible**; the market constraint says what is **available on what terms**. Profit maximisation is the best point in the intersection of the two.

## The model

A competitive firm takes $p$ and $w$ as given and solves

$$\max_{x\ge0}\;\pi=p\,f(x)-w\cdot x$$

**Competitive** matters: because the firm cannot influence prices, $p$ and $w$ are constants when differentiating. A firm with market power would face $p(y)$ and get a different first-order condition.

## The graph

![Isoprofit lines have slope $w/p$. The firm climbs to the highest one still touching the production set — which is the tangency.](content/figures/profit-max.svg)

Put input $x$ on the horizontal axis and output $y$ on the vertical.

- **The production set** is the region under $y=f(x)$ — everything technically feasible.
- **Isoprofit lines** join the plans yielding a given profit. From $\pi=py-wx$,

$$y=\frac{\pi}{p}+\frac{w}{p}\,x$$

so each is a straight line of slope $w/p$ and vertical intercept $\pi/p$. **Higher lines mean higher profit.**

**The solution.** The firm pushes to the highest isoprofit line that still touches the production set. That contact point is a **tangency**: at the optimum the slope of the production function equals the slope of the isoprofit line.

## First-order condition

$$\frac{d\pi}{dx}=p\,f'(x^{*})-w=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\boxed{\;p\,f'(x^{*})=w\;}$$

**Interpretation.** The left side is the **marginal revenue product** — what one more unit of input is worth in output, valued at the market price. The right side is what that unit costs. Hire until the two are equal; before it each unit adds more than it costs, after it less.

Note this *is* the tangency in the graph: $f'(x^{*})=w/p$.

## Second-order condition

$$\frac{d^{2}\pi}{dx^{2}}=p\,f''(x^{*})\le0\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f''(x^{*})\le0$$

since $p>0$. The production function must be **locally concave** — diminishing marginal product — at the optimum.

**What it rules out.** Where $f$ is convex (increasing returns), the stationary point is a profit *minimum*, and profit rises without bound as the firm expands. That is why **no profit-maximising plan exists under increasing returns to scale** if any plan yields positive profit: another exam question that is really this condition.

## Vector notation

With $n$ inputs, $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{+}$:

**FOC** — the gradient of the production function, valued at $p$, equals the factor price vector:

$$\boxed{\;p\,Df(x^{*})=w\;}\qquad\text{that is}\qquad p\frac{\partial f(x^{*})}{\partial x_i}=w_i\quad\text{for }i=1,\dots,n$$

**SOC** — the Hessian of $f$ must be negative semidefinite at $x^{*}$:

$$\boxed{\;h^{\mathsf T}D^{2}f(x^{*})\,h\le0\quad\text{for all }h\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\;}$$

Unlike the consumer's problem there is **no constraint**, so the condition holds for *all* directions $h$, not only those in a budget plane. That is the one structural difference between the two second-order conditions, and it is worth naming.

## The claim

Under **constant returns to scale**, if any feasible plan earns strictly positive profit, then no profit-maximising plan exists. And when a maximum does exist, it is generally **not unique**.

## Existence

**Step 1 — Scaling stays feasible.** Under CRS the production set is a cone: if $(y,-x)\in Y$ then so is $(ty,-tx)$ for every $t>0$. Doubling every input doubles output, and the doubled plan is still technically possible.

**Step 2 — Profit scales with it.** Profit is linear in the plan, so

$$\pi(t)=p\,(ty)-w\cdot(tx)=t\,\big[p\,y-w\cdot x\big]=t\,\pi(1)$$

**Step 3 — The conclusion.** Suppose some feasible plan has $\pi(1)>0$. Then

$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\pi(t)=\lim_{t\to\infty}t\,\pi(1)=+\infty$$

Profit can be made larger without limit simply by operating the same plan at a larger scale. **No plan maximises profit**, because whatever plan you name, doubling it beats it. $\blacksquare$

**So under CRS only three cases arise:**

| Best available $\pi$ | What happens |
|---|---|
| $\pi>0$ | no maximum — profit unbounded |
| $\pi<0$ | shut down; $y=0$ is optimal |
| $\pi=0$ | a maximum exists, at every scale |

**The economic reading.** Long-run competitive equilibrium under CRS therefore *requires* zero profit. If price exceeded minimum average cost, existing firms would expand without limit and entrants would appear. The zero-profit condition is not an assumption bolted on — it is what has to hold for the firm's problem to have an answer at all.

## Uniqueness

Take the surviving case $\pi=0$. Then by Step 2 **every** scaling of that plan also earns exactly zero:

$$\pi(t)=t\cdot0=0\qquad\text{for all }t>0$$

Every point along the ray is a maximiser. The solution is a **whole ray, not a point**, so supply is a **correspondence** rather than a function — the firm is indifferent about its own size, and the individual firm's scale is indeterminate even though the industry's total output is pinned down by demand.

## Increasing returns is worse, and what firms do about it

Under IRS the argument bites harder: profit grows **faster** than proportionally, $\pi(t)>t\,\pi(1)$, so expansion is attractive even when profit is currently negative, provided it turns positive at some scale. Not even the zero-profit case is safe.

The upshot is that **competitive price-taking behaviour is inconsistent with increasing returns**. A firm with IRS expands until it is large relative to the market, at which point it can no longer treat price as given, and the competitive model must be replaced by one with market power. That is why natural monopoly arises in industries with large fixed costs and falling average cost.

## Statement

The profit function

$$\pi(p)=\max_{y\in Y}\;p\cdot y$$

is **convex** in prices: for any $p'$, $p''$ and $t\in[0,1]$,

$$\pi\big(tp'+(1-t)p''\big)\;\le\;t\,\pi(p')+(1-t)\,\pi(p'')$$

## Proof

![At $p^{*}$ the fixed plan is optimal and the two curves touch. Elsewhere the firm re-optimises and does strictly better, so $\pi$ bends upward.](content/figures/profit-convex.svg)

**Step 1 — Set up.** Let $p^{t}=t\,p'+(1-t)\,p''$, and let $y^{t}$ be a profit-maximising plan at those prices, so that $\pi(p^{t})=p^{t}\cdot y^{t}$.

**Step 2 — Split the profit of $y^{t}$.** Using linearity of the inner product:

$$\pi(p^{t})=p^{t}\cdot y^{t}=t\,(p'\cdot y^{t})+(1-t)\,(p''\cdot y^{t})$$

**Step 3 — Feasible but not necessarily optimal.** The plan $y^{t}$ belongs to $Y$, and $Y$ does not change with prices. So $y^{t}$ was *available* at $p'$ and at $p''$ — but the firm need not have chosen it there. Hence its profit cannot exceed the maximum:

$$p'\cdot y^{t}\le\pi(p'),\qquad p''\cdot y^{t}\le\pi(p'')$$

**Step 4 — Combine.**

$$\pi(p^{t})\;\le\;t\,\pi(p')+(1-t)\,\pi(p'')$$

which is convexity. $\blacksquare$

## Reading the proof

Notice the shape of the argument: **hold the plan fixed and profit is a straight line in prices**; let the firm re-optimise and it does at least as well, and usually better. The profit function is therefore the upper envelope of a family of straight lines, and an upper envelope of linear functions is always convex.

This is the same argument that makes the expenditure function **concave** — there the fixed bundle gives an upper straight line and re-optimising lowers cost. One idea, two theorems, opposite curvature because one is a maximum and the other a minimum.

## Two consequences worth stating

**Fluctuating prices are good for a competitive firm.** Convexity gives, by Jensen's inequality,

$$\mathbb{E}\big[\pi(p)\big]\;\ge\;\pi\big(\mathbb{E}[p]\big)$$

Average profit under a fluctuating price is at least as large as profit at the stabilised average price. The firm gains from variability because it can *adapt* — produce more when the price is high, less when it is low. This is exactly the result other papers ask for separately, and it is a one-line corollary of convexity.

**Hotelling's lemma.** Where $\pi$ is differentiable, the slope of the tangent at $p^{*}$ is the optimal plan itself:

$$\frac{\partial\pi(p)}{\partial p_i}=y_i(p)$$

Supply and factor demand are recovered by differentiating the profit function — the firm-side twin of Shephard's lemma.

questions.answer:
## The claim, stated precisely

Let the output price be random with mean $\bar p=\mathbb{E}[p]$. Compare two regimes with the **same average price**:

- **fluctuating** — the firm faces the random $p$ and re-optimises each period;
- **stabilised** — the government fixes the price at $\bar p$ every period.

**Claim.** Average profit under fluctuation is at least as large:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[\pi(p)\big]\;\ge\;\pi\big(\mathbb{E}[p]\big)$$

The equal-mean condition matters: without it the comparison is about the *level* of prices, not their variability.

## The argument

**Step 1 — The profit function is convex in prices.** Hold the production plan fixed and profit is a *straight line* in $p$. Let the firm re-optimise and it does at least as well at every price. So $\pi(p)$ is the **upper envelope of a family of straight lines**, and an upper envelope of linear functions is convex.

![Profit is the upper envelope of the fixed-plan lines, so it bends upward.](content/figures/profit-convex.svg)

**Step 2 — Apply Jensen's inequality.** For any convex function $\varphi$ and random variable $p$,

$$\mathbb{E}\big[\varphi(p)\big]\;\ge\;\varphi\big(\mathbb{E}[p]\big)$$

Setting $\varphi=\pi$ gives the claim directly. $\blacksquare$

**Seeing it on the diagram.** Take two equally likely prices $p_1$ and $p_2$ averaging $\bar p$. Expected profit is the **midpoint of the chord** joining $\pi(p_1)$ and $\pi(p_2)$; stabilised profit is the value of the curve at $\bar p$. Because the curve is convex it lies **below its chords**, so the chord midpoint sits above the curve.

## The intuition

The gain comes entirely from the **freedom to adapt**. When the price is high the firm expands; when it is low it contracts, or shuts down and loses nothing beyond fixed costs. Profit therefore rises *more* in a good period than it falls in an equally bad one — the payoff is asymmetric in the firm's favour.

Stabilising the price removes that option value. The firm produces the same quantity every period and never exploits the good ones.

**A neat corollary:** the gap $\mathbb{E}[\pi(p)]-\pi(\bar p)$ is precisely the **value of flexibility**. The more curved $\pi$ is — the more responsive the technology — the more the firm gains from variability.

## The qualification worth adding

The result is about the **firm's profit**, not welfare, and it assumes:

- **risk neutrality.** The firm maximises expected profit. A risk-averse owner may still prefer the certain price, since the argument ranks expected profits, not expected utility.
- **genuine flexibility.** With output committed in advance — a crop planted before the price is known — the firm cannot re-optimise, profit is linear in price, and Jensen holds with **equality**. The gain from fluctuation vanishes.

That second point explains why real price-stabilisation schemes are so often defended anyway: producers who cannot adjust quickly get none of this benefit and bear all of the risk.

## The technology

$$y=\begin{cases}0 & x\le1\\[2pt] \ln x & x>1\end{cases}$$

The kink matters: the firm produces nothing until it has used one unit of input, so **shutting down is always available** and the answer will have two branches.

## Step 1 — The interior problem

For $x>1$ the firm solves

$$\max_{x}\;\pi=p\ln x-wx$$

**First-order condition.**

$$\frac{d\pi}{dx}=\frac{p}{x}-w=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \boxed{\;x^{*}=\frac{p}{w}\;}$$

**Second-order condition.** $d^{2}\pi/dx^{2}=-p/x^{2}<0$, so this is a maximum. The log technology is strictly concave everywhere, which is why the interior solution is well behaved.

**Output supply.** $y^{*}=\ln x^{*}=\ln(p/w)$.

## Step 2 — Interior profit

Substituting $x^{*}=p/w$:

$$\pi=p\ln\!\left(\frac{p}{w}\right)-w\cdot\frac{p}{w} =p\ln\!\left(\frac{p}{w}\right)-p =p\left[\ln\!\left(\frac{p}{w}\right)-1\right]$$

## Step 3 — Compare with shutting down

Producing nothing gives $\pi=0$. So the firm operates only if the interior profit is positive:

$$p\left[\ln\!\left(\frac{p}{w}\right)-1\right]>0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \ln\!\left(\frac{p}{w}\right)>1 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \boxed{\;\frac{p}{w}>e\;}$$

**This is the answer's real content.** The firm shuts down unless the price is more than $e\approx2.718$ times the input price. A positive marginal product at $x^{*}$ is *not* enough — the firm must also cover the input it had to sink before producing anything at all.

## The profit function

$$\pi(p,w)=\begin{cases} p\left[\ln\!\left(\dfrac{p}{w}\right)-1\right] & \text{if } p>e\,w\\[10pt] 0 & \text{if } p\le e\,w \end{cases}$$

**Worked check.** With $w=1$: at $p=2$ the interior expression gives $-0.61$, so the firm shuts down and $\pi=0$. At $p=3$ it gives $+0.30>0$, so it operates. At $p=10$, $\pi=13.03$. The switch happens between $p=2$ and $p=3$, exactly where $p/w$ crosses $e$.

**Two properties worth noting.** $\pi$ is **continuous** at the threshold — both branches equal zero there, so there is no jump. And it is **convex** in $p$, as every profit function must be: the flat zero branch and the rising curved branch meet without the function ever bending the wrong way.

questions.answer:
## Statement

Consider a maximisation whose solution depends on a parameter $\alpha$:

$$M(\alpha)=\max_{x}\;f(x,\alpha),\qquad\text{with maximiser }x^{*}(\alpha)$$

$M(\alpha)$ is the **value function**. The envelope theorem says that to differentiate it with respect to the parameter, you may **hold the choice variable fixed**:

$$\boxed{\;\frac{dM(\alpha)}{d\alpha}=\frac{\partial f(x,\alpha)}{\partial\alpha}\bigg|_{x=x^{*}(\alpha)}\;}$$

With a constraint the same holds with $f$ replaced by the Lagrangian.

## Why the indirect terms vanish

This is the part worth explaining, since the statement looks too good to be true. Differentiating $M(\alpha)=f\big(x^{*}(\alpha),\alpha\big)$ by the chain rule gives **two** terms:

$$\frac{dM}{d\alpha}=\underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot\frac{dx^{*}}{d\alpha}}_{\text{indirect}}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha}}_{\text{direct}}$$

But $x^{*}$ is a maximiser, so the first-order condition says $\partial f/\partial x=0$ **at that point**. The whole indirect term is multiplied by zero and disappears:

$$\frac{dM}{d\alpha}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\alpha}$$

**The economic reading.** At an optimum the agent is already doing the best they can, so a *marginal* re-optimisation in response to a small parameter change is worth nothing to first order. Only the direct effect of the parameter matters. The adjustment is second-order small.

![The value function is the upper envelope of the fixed-choice curves, and is tangent to one of them at each parameter value.](content/figures/envelope-theorem.svg)

**Where the name comes from.** Each fixed choice of $x$ traces its own curve of $f(x,\alpha)$ against $\alpha$. $M(\alpha)$ is the **upper envelope** of that whole family, touching each member at the parameter value where that choice happens to be optimal. At the point of contact the two are **tangent** — which is exactly the theorem.

## Why it matters in this course

Three central results are one-line corollaries, and saying so is what earns the last mark.

**Hotelling's lemma.** Apply it to $\pi(p,w)=\max_y[p\,y-w\cdot x]$:

$$\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial p}=y(p,w),\qquad -\frac{\partial\pi}{\partial w_i}=x_i(p,w)$$

**Shephard's lemma.** Apply it to $c(w,y)=\min_x w\cdot x$:

$$\frac{\partial c}{\partial w_i}=x_i(w,y)$$

**Roy's identity.** Apply it to $v(p,m)$ with Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}=u(x)+\lambda(m-p\cdot x)$:

$$\frac{\partial v}{\partial p_i}=-\lambda x_i,\quad\frac{\partial v}{\partial m}=\lambda \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_i=-\frac{\partial v/\partial p_i}{\partial v/\partial m}$$

Each recovers an optimal *quantity* by differentiating a *value*, and each is the envelope theorem applied to a different problem. Seeing that turns three separate memorised results into one.

questions.answer:
## The problem and its first-order condition

$$\min_{x}\;w\cdot x\quad\text{s.t.}\quad f(x)=y \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathcal{L}=w\cdot x-\lambda\big(f(x)-y\big)$$

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x_i}=w_i-\lambda\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{w_1}{w_2}=\frac{\partial f/\partial x_1}{\partial f/\partial x_2}=|TRS|$$

**The isoquant is tangent to the isocost line.** That is the geometric content, and everything below is about what happens when you move *away* from that point along the isocost.

![A first-order move along the isocost keeps output constant to first order; the second-order term pulls output strictly below $y$.](content/figures/cost-min.svg)

## The first-order movement leaves output unchanged

Consider a small displacement $dx$ **along the isocost line**, so total cost does not change:

$$w\cdot dx=0$$

The change in output, to first order, is the total differential

$$dy=\sum_i\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}\,dx_i=Df(x^{*})\cdot dx$$

But the first-order condition says $Df(x^{*})=w/\lambda$. Substituting:

$$dy=\frac{1}{\lambda}\,w\cdot dx=\frac{1}{\lambda}\cdot 0=0$$

**Output is unchanged to first order.** Moving a little way along the isocost line takes you along the isoquant as well — the two are tangent, so to first order they coincide. This is exactly why the first-order condition alone cannot tell you whether you are at a minimum: every nearby point on the isocost looks, to first order, like it produces the same output.

## The second-order movement reduces output

Carry the expansion one term further. For a displacement $h$ with $w\cdot h=0$:

$$f(x^{*}+h)\approx f(x^{*})+\underbrace{Df(x^{*})\cdot h}_{=\,0}+\tfrac{1}{2}\,h^{\mathsf T}D^{2}f(x^{*})\,h$$

The first-order term vanishes by the argument above, so the **second-order term decides everything**:

$$f(x^{*}+h)-y\;\approx\;\tfrac{1}{2}\,h^{\mathsf T}D^{2}f(x^{*})\,h$$

The second-order condition for cost minimisation is that this quadratic form is negative for every feasible direction:

$$\boxed{\;h^{\mathsf T}D^{2}f(x^{*})\,h<0\quad\text{for all }h\neq0\text{ with }w\cdot h=0\;}$$

Under it, $f(x^{*}+h)<y$: **output strictly decreases**.

## What this means, and why it is the right condition

**Geometrically.** Move along the isocost line away from the tangency and you slide *off* the isoquant — and because the isoquant is convex, you slide to the inside, where output is lower. The isocost line is a tangent to a convex curve, so apart from the point of contact it lies entirely in the region producing *less* than $y$.

**Why that makes $x^{*}$ a cost minimum.** Turn the statement round. Every other point on that isocost produces less than $y$, so any bundle that *does* produce $y$ must lie on a **higher** isocost line — it must cost more. That is precisely the claim that $x^{*}$ minimises cost subject to producing $y$.

**The link to convexity.** $h^{\mathsf T}D^{2}f\,h<0$ on the constraint set is the analytic statement that the isoquant is convex to the origin, equivalently that $f$ is quasi-concave. Where it fails — a concave stretch of isoquant — the tangency locates a cost *maximum* among the points producing $y$, and the true optimum is at a corner.

questions.answer:
## The concept

**Weak Axiom of Cost Minimization.** If a firm minimises cost, then the bundle it chose at prices $w^{t}$ must be no more expensive, *at those prices*, than any other bundle capable of producing the same output:

$$\boxed{\;w^{t}\cdot x^{t}\;\le\;w^{t}\cdot x^{s}\quad\text{whenever }x^{s}\text{ can also produce }y^{t}\;}$$

**In words.** The firm had the alternative available and did not take it, so what it *did* choose cannot have cost more. WACM is the cost-side analogue of WARP.

## Testing the table

| Obs | $y$ | $w_1$ | $w_2$ | $x_1$ | $x_2$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | 100 | 2 | 1 | 10 | 20 |
| **B** | 110 | 1 | 2 | 14 | 10 |

**Step 1 — Cost each bundle at each price vector.**

$$w^{A}\!\cdot x^{A}=2(10)+1(20)=\mathbf{40} \qquad\qquad w^{A}\!\cdot x^{B}=2(14)+1(10)=\mathbf{38}$$

$$w^{B}\!\cdot x^{B}=1(14)+2(10)=\mathbf{34} \qquad\qquad w^{B}\!\cdot x^{A}=1(10)+2(20)=\mathbf{50}$$

**Step 2 — Deal with the different output levels.** WACM compares bundles producing the *same* output, and here $y^{A}=100$ while $y^{B}=110$. But $y^{B}>y^{A}$, so under **monotonicity** the bundle $x^{B}$ produces at least 110, and therefore certainly at least 100:

$$x^{B}\in V(100)$$

So $x^{B}$ *was* an available way of producing $100$, and the comparison at $A$'s prices is legitimate. (The reverse comparison is not: $x^{A}$ produces only 100 and cannot be assumed to reach 110, which is why the $B$ row proves nothing.)

**Step 3 — Apply the axiom.**

$$\text{Required at }w^{A}:\quad w^{A}\!\cdot x^{A}\le w^{A}\!\cdot x^{B} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 40\le 38\quad\textbf{FALSE}$$

$$\text{At }w^{B}:\quad 34\le 50\quad\text{holds, but is uninformative for the reason above}$$

## Verdict

**The behaviour is NOT consistent with cost minimisation.** At observation $A$'s prices $(2,1)$ the firm spent 40 to produce 100 units, when the bundle $x^{B}=(14,10)$ would have cost only 38 at those same prices and would have produced **more** — at least 110 units. A cost-minimising firm could not have made that choice.

The violation is decisive: it needs no assumption about the shape of the technology, only monotonicity.

## The general result behind the test

Where output *is* the same across observations, adding the two WACM inequalities gives the standard comparative-static prediction. From

$$w^{t}\!\cdot x^{t}\le w^{t}\!\cdot x^{s}\qquad\text{and}\qquad w^{s}\!\cdot x^{s}\le w^{s}\!\cdot x^{t}$$

add and rearrange:

$$(w^{t}-w^{s})\cdot(x^{t}-x^{s})\le0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\boxed{\;\Delta w\,\Delta x\le0\;}$$

Taking one price at a time, $\Delta w_i\,\Delta x_i\le0$: **conditional factor demand curves slope downward.** As with WAPM on the profit side, the prediction follows from the axiom alone — no differentiability, no convexity, no functional form.

questions.text: Suppose we consider the cost minimization problem of a firm with Cobb-Douglas technology given by $y=Ax_1^{a}x_2^{b}$. Derive the cost function for this firm. (7.5)
answerPoints: State the constrained minimisation problem and the Lagrangian — 1.5 marks

questions.answer:
> **The result.**
> $$c(w,y)=(a+b)\left(\frac{y}{A}\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b}}\left(\frac{w_1}{a}\right)^{\frac{a}{a+b}}\left(\frac{w_2}{b}\right)^{\frac{b}{a+b}}$$

## Step 1 — The problem

The firm must produce a *given* output $y$ at least cost:

$$c(w,y)=\min_{x_1,x_2}\;w_1x_1+w_2x_2\quad\text{s.t.}\quad Ax_1^{a}x_2^{b}=y$$

Note what is fixed and what is chosen: output is a **constraint**, not a choice. This is why the solutions are called *conditional* factor demands — conditional on producing $y$.

$$\mathcal{L}=w_1x_1+w_2x_2-\lambda\left(Ax_1^{a}x_2^{b}-y\right)$$

## Step 2 — First-order conditions

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x_1}=w_1-\lambda A a\,x_1^{a-1}x_2^{b}=0$$
$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x_2}=w_2-\lambda A b\,x_1^{a}x_2^{b-1}=0$$

## Step 3 — The tangency condition

Divide the first by the second; $\lambda$ and $A$ cancel:

$$\frac{w_1}{w_2}=\frac{a\,x_2}{b\,x_1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \underbrace{\frac{MP_1}{MP_2}}_{|TRS|}=\frac{w_1}{w_2}$$

**Say what this means.** At the cost-minimising point the isoquant is tangent to the isocost line. If the two differed, the firm could substitute along the isoquant — same output, lower cost — so it would not be optimal.

Rearranged for substitution:

$$x_2=\frac{b}{a}\cdot\frac{w_1}{w_2}\,x_1$$

## Step 4 — Conditional factor demands

Put that into the constraint $Ax_1^{a}x_2^{b}=y$:

$$A\,x_1^{a}\left(\frac{b\,w_1}{a\,w_2}x_1\right)^{b}=y\;\Longrightarrow\;A\left(\frac{b\,w_1}{a\,w_2}\right)^{b}x_1^{a+b}=y$$

$$\boxed{\;x_1(w,y)=\left(\frac{y}{A}\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b}}\left(\frac{a\,w_2}{b\,w_1}\right)^{\frac{b}{a+b}}\;}$$

and symmetrically

$$\boxed{\;x_2(w,y)=\left(\frac{y}{A}\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b}}\left(\frac{b\,w_1}{a\,w_2}\right)^{\frac{a}{a+b}}\;}$$

## Step 5 — The cost function

Rather than substituting both demands and grinding through, use the tangency relation. Since $w_2x_2=\frac{b}{a}w_1x_1$:

$$c=w_1x_1+w_2x_2=w_1x_1\left(1+\frac{b}{a}\right)=\frac{a+b}{a}\,w_1x_1$$

Substituting $x_1$ from step 4 and collecting the powers:

$$c(w,y)=\frac{a+b}{a}\,w_1\left(\frac{y}{A}\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b}}\left(\frac{a\,w_2}{b\,w_1}\right)^{\frac{b}{a+b}}$$

Since $1-\frac{b}{a+b}=\frac{a}{a+b}$, the $w_1$ powers combine to $w_1^{a/(a+b)}$ and the $a$ terms to $a^{-a/(a+b)}$:

$$\boxed{\;c(w,y)=(a+b)\left(\frac{y}{A}\right)^{\frac{1}{a+b}}\left(\frac{w_1}{a}\right)^{\frac{a}{a+b}}\left(\frac{w_2}{b}\right)^{\frac{b}{a+b}}\;}$$

## Step 6 — Check the result

**Homogeneity.** Doubling both factor prices doubles cost — the exponents on $w_1$ and $w_2$ sum to $\frac{a}{a+b}+\frac{b}{a+b}=1$, so $c$ is homogeneous of degree one in $w$, as every cost function must be.

**Shephard's lemma.** $\partial c/\partial w_1$ should return $x_1(w,y)$. Differentiating brings down $\frac{a}{a+b}$ and reduces the $w_1$ exponent by one, reproducing step 4 exactly.

**Returns to scale, read off the exponent on $y$.** Cost rises with $y^{1/(a+b)}$, so:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| $a+b=1$ | constant returns | $c$ is linear in $y$; average cost flat |
| $a+b>1$ | increasing returns | $c$ concave in $y$; average cost falling |
| $a+b<1$ | decreasing returns | $c$ convex in $y$; average cost rising |

That single exponent carries the entire returns-to-scale story, which is the most useful sentence in the answer.

## The two cost concepts

**Short run.** Some input is fixed — call it plant size $k$. The firm minimises cost over the variable inputs only:

$$c_{s}(w,y,k)=\min_{x}\;\{w\cdot x\;:\;f(x,k)=y\}$$

**Long run.** Everything varies, including $k$:

$$c(w,y)=\min_{k}\;c_{s}(w,y,k)$$

**The inequality is immediate.** The long run minimises over a strictly larger set of choices, so

$$c(w,y)\le c_{s}(w,y,k)\qquad\text{for every }k$$

with **equality** at the $k$ that is optimal for that particular $y$. Write that optimal plant size $k^{*}(y)$.

## The tangency

At $y_0$, choose the plant $k^{*}(y_0)$. Then $c(w,y_0)=c_{s}(w,y_0,k^{*}(y_0))$ — the two curves **touch**. Away from $y_0$ the same fixed plant is no longer the right size, so the short-run curve rises above the long-run one. Touching at one point and lying above elsewhere is exactly **tangency**.

Dividing by $y$ carries the relationship to the average curves: $LAC(y)\le SAC(y,k)$, with equality at $y_0$.

**So the LAC is the lower envelope of the family of SAC curves** — one SAC for each plant size, and the LAC tracing the bottom of them all. It is often called the *planning curve*: it tells you the cheapest way to produce each output once you are free to choose the plant.

## Where the envelope theorem enters

Differentiate the long-run cost with respect to output. Since $k^{*}(y)$ is itself chosen optimally,

$$\frac{dc(w,y)}{dy}=\frac{\partial c_{s}(w,y,k)}{\partial y}\bigg|_{k=k^{*}(y)}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial c_{s}}{\partial k}\cdot\frac{dk^{*}}{dy}}_{=\,0}$$

The second term vanishes because $k^{*}$ minimises $c_s$ over $k$, so $\partial c_{s}/\partial k=0$ there. Hence

$$\boxed{\;LMC(y)=SMC\big(y,k^{*}(y)\big)\;}$$

**Long-run marginal cost equals short-run marginal cost at the optimal plant.** This is the envelope theorem in its purest form: adjusting the plant is worth nothing *to first order*, because the plant was already the right size.

## The consequence students most often get wrong

The LAC is tangent to each SAC — but **not at the SAC's own minimum**, except at one point.

- On the **falling** stretch of the LAC, tangency occurs to the **left** of the SAC minimum.
- On the **rising** stretch, tangency occurs to the **right** of it.
- Only at the **minimum of the LAC** do the two minima coincide, and that plant is the *optimal scale*.

The reason is geometric: tangency requires the slopes to match, and where the LAC slopes downward the SAC must be sloping downward too — which cannot be at its own lowest point.

questions.answer:
## (a) What local nonsatiation says

**Definition.** Preferences are *locally nonsatiated* if for every bundle $x$ and every distance $\varepsilon>0$, however small, there is some bundle $y$ within that distance which is strictly preferred:

$$\forall x,\;\forall \varepsilon>0,\;\;\exists\,y \text{ with } \lVert y-x\rVert<\varepsilon \;\text{ such that }\; y\succ x$$

**In plain words.** Wherever you stand, there is something better within arm's reach. You can never be at a spot where every nearby bundle is only as good or worse.

Two things it does **not** say. It does not require *more of everything* to be better — monotonicity is a stronger assumption. And it does not rule out bads: the improving bundle $y$ may involve *less* of something. Local nonsatiation is the weak assumption that does the work.

**Why we assume it.** It forces the budget constraint to hold with equality. If the consumer left money unspent, local nonsatiation would supply a strictly better affordable bundle nearby, contradicting optimality. That is what lets us write $p\cdot x=m$ rather than $p\cdot x\le m$ throughout.

## (b) Why thick indifference curves cannot survive it

![Left: inside a thick band every nearby bundle is merely indifferent, so no improvement exists. Right: on a thin curve, an improving bundle sits in every neighbourhood.](content/figures/local-nonsatiation.svg)

**Proof by contradiction — four steps.**

**1. Suppose a thick indifference curve exists.** "Thick" means the indifference set contains a band of positive width rather than a curve of zero thickness. Formally, there is a bundle $x$ and a radius $\delta>0$ such that every bundle $y$ with $\lVert y-x\rVert<\delta$ is *indifferent* to $x$:

$$y\sim x\quad\text{for all } y \text{ in the ball } B_\delta(x)$$

**2. Apply local nonsatiation at that $x$.** Take $\varepsilon=\delta$. Local nonsatiation guarantees some $y$ with $\lVert y-x\rVert<\delta$ and $y\succ x$.

**3. The contradiction.** That $y$ lies inside the ball, so by step 1 it must satisfy $y\sim x$. But step 2 says $y\succ x$. A bundle cannot be both strictly better than $x$ and indifferent to it — the two relations are mutually exclusive.

**4. Conclude.** The supposition in step 1 is false. No such thick band can exist, so every indifference set has empty interior: indifference curves are **thin**.

## Why this matters beyond the proof

A thick indifference curve would wreck the theory in three concrete ways, and naming one lifts the answer above bookwork:

- **The optimum stops being a point.** Tangency with the budget line would pick out a whole region, so demand becomes a correspondence rather than a function.
- **The expenditure function breaks.** With a band of indifferent bundles there is no well-defined *minimum* cost of reaching utility $u$.
- **Duality fails.** $v$ and $e$ would no longer be inverses, and Shephard's lemma needs a unique cost-minimising bundle to differentiate to.

**Conclusion.** Local nonsatiation is the minimal assumption that makes the budget bind and indifference curves thin — and those two facts are what the entire apparatus of $x$, $v$, $e$ and $h$ rests on.

## (c) The properties of $v(p,m)$

$v(p,m)=\max\{u(x):p\cdot x\le m\}$ is the **maximum utility attainable**. It has five properties:

1. **Non-increasing in $p$.** If $p'\ge p$ then $v(p',m)\le v(p,m)$. Raising a price shrinks the budget set, and a smaller feasible set cannot yield more utility.
2. **Increasing in $m$.** More income enlarges the budget set. Strictly increasing under local nonsatiation.
3. **Homogeneous of degree zero in $(p,m)$.** $v(tp,tm)=v(p,m)$ for $t>0$ — scaling all prices and income leaves the budget set literally unchanged, so nothing real has happened. This is the formal statement that there is **no money illusion**.
4. **Quasiconvex in $p$.** $\{p:v(p,m)\le k\}$ is convex for every $k$. Proved in (d).
5. **Continuous** in $p$ and $m$, for $p\gg0$, $m>0$.

## (d) Proof that $v$ is quasiconvex in $p$

![The set of prices leaving the consumer no better off than $k$ is convex — a chord between any two of its points stays inside.](content/figures/quasiconvex-v.svg)

**What must be shown.** Take any two price vectors $p'$ and $p''$ with

$$v(p',m)\le k\qquad\text{and}\qquad v(p'',m)\le k$$

and let $p^{t}=t\,p'+(1-t)\,p''$ for $t\in[0,1]$. We must show $v(p^{t},m)\le k$.

**Step 1 — Take the optimal bundle at the averaged prices.** Let $x$ be a bundle that is affordable at $p^{t}$, so

$$p^{t}\cdot x\le m,\qquad\text{that is}\qquad t\,(p'\cdot x)+(1-t)(p''\cdot x)\le m$$

**Step 2 — The key observation.** The left-hand side is a weighted average of $p'\cdot x$ and $p''\cdot x$ with weights summing to one. An average cannot be smaller than both of the things averaged, so **at least one** of the two must be no greater than $m$:

$$p'\cdot x\le m\qquad\text{or}\qquad p''\cdot x\le m$$

If both exceeded $m$, their weighted average would exceed $m$ too — contradicting Step 1.

**Step 3 — Apply the hypothesis.** Suppose without loss of generality that $p'\cdot x\le m$. Then $x$ was affordable at prices $p'$, so it cannot deliver more than the best available there:

$$u(x)\le v(p',m)\le k$$

**Step 4 — Conclude.** Every bundle affordable at $p^{t}$ yields utility at most $k$. Hence the best of them does too:

$$v(p^{t},m)\le k$$

So $p^{t}$ lies in the set, the set is convex, and $v$ is quasiconvex in $p$. $\blacksquare$

## The two remarks that lift the answer

**Quasiconvex, not convex.** The theorem is about the *shape of the level sets*, not the curvature of the function. $v$ itself need not be a convex function of $p$ — Cobb-Douglas $v=m\,a^{a}(1-a)^{1-a}p_1^{-a}p_2^{-(1-a)}$ is not. Candidates who claim convexity have proved something false.

**The economic reading.** Averaging two price vectors cannot make the consumer better off than the better of the two originals. Price *variability* is, in this sense, not something the consumer gains from — the mirror image of the firm's profit function, which is genuinely **convex** in prices because the firm can re-optimise and so *does* gain from variability.

## The graph

![The optimum is where the highest reachable indifference curve just touches the budget line.](content/figures/consumer-equilibrium.svg)

Draw $x_1$ and $x_2$ on the axes. Two objects go on the diagram:

- **The budget line** $p_1x_1+p_2x_2=m$, with intercepts $m/p_1$ and $m/p_2$ and slope $-p_1/p_2$. Everything on or below it is affordable.
- **The indifference map**, convex to the origin, higher curves meaning higher utility.

**Reading the optimum off the picture.** The consumer wants the highest curve that still touches the budget set. A curve cutting *through* the budget line cannot be optimal — part of it lies inside the budget set, so a better affordable bundle exists just along it. A curve lying entirely above the line is unaffordable. The best attainable is the one that is **tangent**.

## The tangency condition

At the point of tangency the two slopes are equal:

$$\underbrace{\left|\frac{dx_2}{dx_1}\right|_{u}}_{MRS}=\frac{MU_1}{MU_2}=\frac{p_1}{p_2}$$

**Say what it means.** The left side is the rate at which the consumer is *willing* to trade good 2 for good 1; the right side is the rate at which the market *lets* them. If $MRS>p_1/p_2$ the consumer values good 1 more highly than it costs, so buying more of it raises utility — and they keep going until the two rates agree.

Rearranged, it says the **marginal utility per taka is equalised** across goods:

$$\frac{MU_1}{p_1}=\frac{MU_2}{p_2}=\lambda$$

## First-order condition in vector notation

The problem is $\max_x u(x)$ subject to $p\cdot x=m$, with Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}=u(x)-\lambda(p\cdot x-m)$. Differentiating:

$$\boxed{\;Du(x^{*})=\lambda\,p\;}\qquad\text{together with}\qquad p\cdot x^{*}=m$$

where $Du(x^{*})=\big(\partial u/\partial x_1,\dots,\partial u/\partial x_n\big)$ is the **gradient vector**.

**Read the vector statement.** It says the gradient of the utility function is *proportional to the price vector* — the direction of steepest utility increase points straight out along the prices. Since the gradient is normal to the indifference surface and $p$ is normal to the budget plane, the two surfaces are tangent. That is the same geometric fact as the picture, stated in $n$ dimensions.

## Second-order condition in vector notation

Tangency alone identifies a stationary point; it could be a minimum. The second-order condition requires the Hessian of $u$ to be **negative semidefinite on the budget plane** — not everywhere, only in directions the consumer can actually move:

$$\boxed{\;h^{\mathsf T}\,D^{2}u(x^{*})\,h\le0\quad\text{for every }h\text{ with }p\cdot h=0\;}$$

The restriction $p\cdot h=0$ picks out the displacements that keep spending equal to $m$.

Equivalently, in bordered-Hessian form, the optimum requires

$$\begin{vmatrix}0 & p^{\mathsf T}\\ p & D^{2}u(x^{*})\end{vmatrix}>0 \qquad\text{(two-good case)}$$

**What it means.** The condition is the analytic content of "indifference curves are convex to the origin". With strictly convex preferences it holds automatically, the tangency point is a genuine maximum, and it is unique — which is what makes demand a **function** rather than a correspondence.

**One caveat worth a line.** All of this assumes an **interior** solution. If the tangency would require a negative quantity, the optimum is at a corner, the FOC holds as an inequality $Du(x^{*})\le\lambda p$, and $MRS$ need not equal the price ratio.

## The properties of $e(p,u)$

$e(p,u)=\min\{p\cdot x:u(x)\ge u\}$ is the **minimum expenditure** needed to reach utility $u$. Five properties:

1. **Non-decreasing in $p$.** If $p'\ge p$ then $e(p',u)\ge e(p,u)$ — reaching the same utility cannot get cheaper when a price rises.
2. **Homogeneous of degree one in $p$.** $e(tp,u)=t\,e(p,u)$. Double every price and you need exactly double the money; the cost-minimising bundle is unchanged.
3. **Concave in $p$.** Shown below.
4. **Continuous** in $p$ for $p\gg0$.
5. **Increasing in $u$**, and by **Shephard's lemma** $\partial e/\partial p_i=h_i(p,u)$ — the price-derivative *is* the Hicksian demand.

## Proof that $e$ is concave in prices

![At $p^{*}$ the fixed bundle is optimal and the two curves touch. Everywhere else re-optimising costs less, so $e$ lies below the straight line.](content/figures/expenditure-concave.svg)

**The idea in one sentence.** Compare the true minimum cost with the cost of a bundle held fixed. The fixed-bundle cost is a *straight line* in prices; the true minimum is never above it, and touches it at one point. A function lying below a family of tangent lines is concave.

**Step 1 — Set up.** Take prices $p'$ and $p''$, and let

$$p^{t}=t\,p'+(1-t)\,p''\qquad t\in[0,1]$$

Let $x^{t}$ be the bundle that minimises expenditure at $p^{t}$ subject to $u(x)\ge u$.

**Step 2 — Split the cost of $x^{t}$.** By definition of $p^{t}$, and using linearity of the inner product:

$$e(p^{t},u)=p^{t}\cdot x^{t}=t\,(p'\cdot x^{t})+(1-t)(p''\cdot x^{t})$$

**Step 3 — Feasible but not necessarily optimal.** The bundle $x^{t}$ reaches utility $u$, so it is **feasible** in the minimisation problem at $p'$ and at $p''$. But it need not be **optimal** there. So its cost is at least the minimum:

$$p'\cdot x^{t}\ge e(p',u),\qquad p''\cdot x^{t}\ge e(p'',u)$$

**Step 4 — Combine.** Substituting these into Step 2:

$$e(p^{t},u)\;\ge\;t\,e(p',u)+(1-t)\,e(p'',u)$$

which is exactly the definition of a **concave** function. $\blacksquare$

## Explaining it

The economic content is the **value of being able to adapt**. If the consumer were locked into the bundle $x^{*}$, their cost would rise linearly with any price — the straight line in the figure. Because they may substitute away from whatever has become expensive, their actual cost rises *more slowly* than that line. Concavity is the curvature that flexibility buys.

**Two consequences worth naming.**

- Differentiating twice, the Hessian of $e$ is negative semidefinite. By Shephard's lemma that Hessian is the **Slutsky matrix**, so this proof is where "the compensated own-price effect is non-positive" ultimately comes from.
- Because $e$ is homogeneous of degree one in $p$, Euler's theorem makes the Hessian **singular**: it is negative *semi*definite and never negative definite. The zero eigenvalue corresponds to scaling all prices at once, which changes no real quantity.

questions.answer:
## What is being assumed *about*

Consumer theory does not start with a utility function. It starts with a **preference relation** $\succsim$, read "is at least as good as", defined over consumption bundles. The four assumptions are the conditions this relation must satisfy before we are entitled to replace it with a number.

## The four assumptions

**1. Completeness.** For any two bundles $x$ and $y$, either $x\succsim y$ or $y\succsim x$ (possibly both).

*What it does:* guarantees the consumer can always compare. Without it some pairs are simply incomparable — the consumer cannot say which is better *or* that they are indifferent — and choice is undefined for those pairs.

**2. Reflexivity.** $x\succsim x$ for every bundle.

*What it does:* every bundle is at least as good as itself. Trivial, and deliberately so; it is a technical requirement for $\succsim$ to be an ordering, not an economic claim.

**3. Transitivity.** If $x\succsim y$ and $y\succsim z$, then $x\succsim z$.

*What it does:* this is the one carrying real weight. Without it, preferences can **cycle**:

$$x\succ y,\qquad y\succ z,\qquad z\succ x$$

and then the set $\{x,y,z\}$ has **no best element** — whichever you name, something in the set beats it. Maximisation becomes meaningless. Transitivity is what makes "choose the best available bundle" a coherent instruction.

**4. Continuity.** For any $y$, the sets $\{x:x\succsim y\}$ and $\{x:x\precsim y\}$ are **closed**.

*What it does:* rules out sudden jumps in preference — a bundle cannot be strictly preferred while bundles arbitrarily close to it are strictly worse.

*The counterexample worth naming:* **lexicographic preferences**, where the consumer ranks first by $x_1$ and turns to $x_2$ only to break ties. These are complete, reflexive and transitive but **not continuous**, and the consequence is severe — they admit **no utility representation at all**, not even a badly behaved one.

## What the four together buy

**Representation theorem.** A preference ordering that is complete, reflexive, transitive and continuous can be represented by a **continuous utility function** $u$, meaning

$$u(x)\ge u(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\succsim y$$

Two remarks earn the last marks. Utility is **ordinal**: any increasing transformation $f(u(x))$ represents the *same* preferences, so the numbers themselves carry no meaning, only the ranking.

And note what is *not* on this list — **monotonicity** and **convexity** are assumed separately, when we want downward-sloping indifference curves and a unique optimum. They are not needed for a utility function to exist.

> **The whole answer in one box.** Everything below is these six lines. Derive them in this order and each one falls out of the last.
>
> $$x_1=\frac{am}{p_1},\qquad x_2=\frac{(1-a)m}{p_2}$$
> $$v(p,m)=m\,\frac{a^{a}(1-a)^{1-a}}{p_1^{a}p_2^{1-a}},\qquad e(p,u)=u\left(\frac{p_1}{a}\right)^{a}\left(\frac{p_2}{1-a}\right)^{1-a}$$
> $$h_1=u\left(\frac{a\,p_2}{(1-a)p_1}\right)^{1-a},\qquad h_2=u\left(\frac{(1-a)p_1}{a\,p_2}\right)^{a}$$

![The four objects of consumer theory. Solve the left column, then walk an arrow — you never solve the same problem twice.](content/figures/duality-map.svg)

## Step 1 — Set up the problem

Maximise utility subject to the budget:

$$\max_{x_1,x_2}\; x_1^{a}x_2^{1-a}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad p_1x_1+p_2x_2=m$$

The budget binds with equality because Cobb-Douglas is strictly increasing in both goods — **local nonsatiation**, so no money is left unspent.

Form the Lagrangian:

$$\mathcal{L}=x_1^{a}x_2^{1-a}-\lambda\,(p_1x_1+p_2x_2-m)$$

## Step 2 — First-order conditions

$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x_1}=a\,x_1^{a-1}x_2^{1-a}-\lambda p_1=0$$
$$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial x_2}=(1-a)\,x_1^{a}x_2^{-a}-\lambda p_2=0$$

Divide the first by the second. The $\lambda$ cancels, and so does most of the algebra:

$$\underbrace{\frac{a}{1-a}\cdot\frac{x_2}{x_1}}_{MRS}=\frac{p_1}{p_2}$$

**This is the tangency condition** — the indifference curve's slope equals the budget line's slope. Say so explicitly; examiners award the interpretation, not just the algebra.

Rearranged, it gives the expenditure split:

$$p_1x_1=\frac{a}{1-a}\,p_2x_2$$

## Step 3 — Marshallian demands

Substitute into the budget constraint $p_1x_1+p_2x_2=m$:

$$\frac{a}{1-a}p_2x_2+p_2x_2=m\;\Longrightarrow\;p_2x_2\left(\frac{a+1-a}{1-a}\right)=m$$

$$\boxed{\;x_1(p,m)=\frac{am}{p_1},\qquad x_2(p,m)=\frac{(1-a)m}{p_2}\;}$$

**Read what this says.** The consumer spends the constant share $a$ of income on good 1 and $1-a$ on good 2, whatever the prices. That constant-budget-share property is the signature of Cobb-Douglas — it is worth one sentence in the answer.

Note also: demand for good 1 does not depend on $p_2$ at all. Cross-price effects are zero here.

## Step 4 — Indirect utility

$v(p,m)$ is the *maximum utility attainable* at prices $p$ and income $m$. Get it by putting the optimal bundle back into $u$:

$$v(p,m)=\left(\frac{am}{p_1}\right)^{a}\left(\frac{(1-a)m}{p_2}\right)^{1-a}$$

Collect the $m$ terms — the exponents sum to $a+(1-a)=1$, so they give exactly one power of $m$:

$$\boxed{\;v(p,m)=m\,\frac{a^{a}(1-a)^{1-a}}{p_1^{a}\,p_2^{1-a}}\;}$$

**Check it against the properties you are asked for elsewhere.** It is decreasing in each price, increasing in $m$, and homogeneous of degree zero: double $p$ and $m$ together and $v$ is unchanged, because the numerator and denominator each pick up one factor of the scalar.

## Step 5 — Expenditure function

$e(p,u)$ is the *minimum income needed* to reach utility $u$. It is the same relationship read the other way round, so set $v(p,m)=u$ and solve for $m$:

$$u=m\,\frac{a^{a}(1-a)^{1-a}}{p_1^{a}p_2^{1-a}}$$

$$\boxed{\;e(p,u)=u\left(\frac{p_1}{a}\right)^{a}\left(\frac{p_2}{1-a}\right)^{1-a}\;}$$

**Why the inversion is legitimate** — worth a line. $v$ is strictly increasing in $m$, so it is one-to-one in $m$ and can be inverted. Hence $e(p,v(p,m))=m$ and $v(p,e(p,u))=u$: the two functions are inverses in their last argument. That is the *duality* the question is really testing.

$e$ is homogeneous of degree **one** in prices: double all prices and you need exactly double the money.

## Step 6 — Hicksian demands, by Shephard's lemma

Shephard's lemma says the compensated demand is the price-derivative of the expenditure function:

$$h_i(p,u)=\frac{\partial e(p,u)}{\partial p_i}$$

Differentiating $e$ with respect to $p_1$ (the $p_2$ factor is a constant here):

$$\boxed{\;h_1(p,u)=u\left(\frac{a\,p_2}{(1-a)p_1}\right)^{1-a},\qquad h_2(p,u)=u\left(\frac{(1-a)p_1}{a\,p_2}\right)^{a}\;}$$

**The consistency check that earns the mark.** Substituting $m=e(p,u)$ into the Marshallian demand must reproduce the Hicksian one:

$$x_1\big(p,e(p,u)\big)=\frac{a\,e(p,u)}{p_1}=u\left(\frac{a p_2}{(1-a)p_1}\right)^{1-a}=h_1(p,u)\;\checkmark$$

## Step 7 — The two money metric functions

These are the parts most candidates drop, and they are quick.

**Money metric direct utility function** $m(p,x)$ — *how much money would this consumer need, at prices $p$, to be exactly as well off as the bundle $x$ makes them?*

$$m(p,x)=e\big(p,u(x)\big)=x_1^{a}x_2^{1-a}\left(\frac{p_1}{a}\right)^{a}\left(\frac{p_2}{1-a}\right)^{1-a}$$

**Money metric indirect utility function** $\mu(p;q,m)$ — *how much money at prices $p$ makes them as well off as income $m$ did at prices $q$?*

$$\mu(p;q,m)=e\big(p,v(q,m)\big)=m\,\frac{a^{a}(1-a)^{1-a}}{q_1^{a}q_2^{1-a}}\left(\frac{p_1}{a}\right)^{a}\left(\frac{p_2}{1-a}\right)^{1-a}$$

Both are just $e$ with its utility argument supplied by $u$ or by $v$. Both are **increasing monotonic transformations** of the underlying utility, which is what makes them legitimate utility representations measured in money.

## The one-line conclusion

All six objects come from one optimisation. Solve the utility-maximisation problem once, substitute back for $v$, invert for $e$, differentiate for $h$ — the duality diagram above is the whole answer in picture form, and stating it that way tells the examiner you understand the structure rather than having memorised four formulas.

## The proposition

Consider the two problems

$$\text{(UMP)}\quad\max_x u(x)\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ p\cdot x\le m \qquad\qquad \text{(EMP)}\quad\min_x p\cdot x\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ u(x)\ge u$$

**Claim.** If $x^{*}$ solves the UMP at $(p,m)$, and $u^{*}=u(x^{*})$, then $x^{*}$ solves the EMP at $(p,u^{*})$ — and the minimised expenditure is exactly $m$.

**Assumed:** $u$ continuous, preferences locally non-satiated, and both problems have solutions.

## Proof by contradiction

**Step 1 — Suppose not.** Let $x^{*}$ solve the UMP but *fail* to solve the EMP. Then some bundle $x'$ reaches the same utility more cheaply:

$$u(x')\ge u^{*}\qquad\text{and}\qquad p\cdot x'<p\cdot x^{*}\le m$$

**Step 2 — Note the strict inequality.** Because $p\cdot x'<m$ *strictly*, the bundle $x'$ lies in the **interior** of the budget set. There is room to spend a little more and still be affordable.

**Step 3 — Apply local nonsatiation.** This is the step the whole proof turns on. Local nonsatiation says that in *every* neighbourhood of $x'$ there is a bundle $x''$ with

$$x''\succ x'\qquad\text{that is}\qquad u(x'')>u(x')$$

Choose the neighbourhood small enough that $x''$ is still affordable — possible precisely because Step 2 left slack.

**Step 4 — The contradiction.** We now have a bundle $x''$ that is **affordable**, $p\cdot x''\le m$, and satisfies

$$u(x'')>u(x')\ge u^{*}=u(x^{*})$$

So $x''$ is affordable and strictly better than $x^{*}$. But $x^{*}$ was assumed to *maximise* utility over the budget set. Contradiction.

Hence no such $x'$ exists, and $x^{*}$ does solve the EMP. $\blacksquare$

**The corollary.** Local nonsatiation also forces the budget to bind at the UMP optimum, so $p\cdot x^{*}=m$ and therefore

$$e(p,u^{*})=m,\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad e\big(p,v(p,m)\big)=m$$

## Where the assumption is indispensable

Drop local nonsatiation and the theorem is **false**. Imagine a consumer fully satiated at $x^{*}$ while $p\cdot x^{*}<m$ — extra income buys nothing they want. Then $x^{*}$ still maximises utility, but it does not minimise the cost of reaching $u^{*}$: some cheaper bundle reaches the same satiated level. Step 3 fails because there is no better bundle nearby to move to.

This is the reason the assumption is stated as *local* nonsatiation rather than monotonicity. It is the weakest condition that closes the argument, and duality — Roy's identity, Shephard's lemma, the Slutsky equation — all rest on the two problems having the same solution.

## (A) What the MRS is

The **marginal rate of substitution** is the rate at which a consumer is *willing* to give up good 2 to obtain one more unit of good 1, **holding utility constant**. Geometrically it is the slope of the indifference curve.

**Derivation.** Take the total differential of $u(x_1,x_2)$ and set it to zero, since moving along an indifference curve leaves utility unchanged:

$$du=\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_1}dx_1+\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_2}dx_2=0$$

Rearranging:

$$\boxed{\;MRS=\frac{dx_2}{dx_1}\bigg|_{u}=-\frac{\partial u/\partial x_1}{\partial u/\partial x_2}=-\frac{MU_1}{MU_2}\;}$$

**Reading it.** The MRS is the **negative ratio of marginal utilities**. It is negative because the curve slopes downward: taking more of good 1 requires giving up some of good 2 to stay equally well off. Textbooks often quote $|MRS|$ and leave the sign implicit.

At an interior optimum the consumer sets $|MRS|=p_1/p_2$ — what they are *willing* to trade equals what the market *lets* them trade.

## (B) The MRS is unchanged by a monotonic transformation

**What must be shown.** Let $v(x_1,x_2)=f\big(u(x_1,x_2)\big)$ where $f$ is a strictly increasing function, so $f'>0$. Show that $v$ and $u$ have the same MRS everywhere.

**Step 1 — Differentiate the transformed function.** By the chain rule:

$$\frac{\partial v}{\partial x_1}=f'\big(u\big)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_1},\qquad\qquad \frac{\partial v}{\partial x_2}=f'\big(u\big)\cdot\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_2}$$

**Step 2 — Form the MRS for $v$.**

$$MRS_v=-\frac{\partial v/\partial x_1}{\partial v/\partial x_2}=-\frac{f'(u)\cdot\partial u/\partial x_1}{f'(u)\cdot\partial u/\partial x_2}$$

**Step 3 — Cancel.** Since $f'(u)>0$ it is non-zero, and it appears identically in numerator and denominator:

$$MRS_v=-\frac{\partial u/\partial x_1}{\partial u/\partial x_2}=MRS_u\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Worked check.** Take $u=x_1^{a}x_2^{1-a}$, for which $MRS=-\dfrac{a\,x_2}{(1-a)\,x_1}$. Now take $v=\ln u=a\ln x_1+(1-a)\ln x_2$:

$$MRS_v=-\frac{a/x_1}{(1-a)/x_2}=-\frac{a\,x_2}{(1-a)\,x_1}$$

Identical, despite $v$ being a completely different function of the bundle.

## Why this result matters

It is the formal content of **ordinal utility**. The marginal utilities $MU_1$ and $MU_2$ each change when you transform $u$ — they are *not* meaningful magnitudes. Their **ratio** does not.

Since the entire theory of consumer choice is built on that ratio — the tangency condition, the demand functions, the Slutsky equation — none of it depends on which particular utility representation was chosen. **Observable behaviour is invariant to the transformation, and so it should be**: nothing the consumer does could ever reveal whether their utility is $u$ or $\ln u$.

## Step 1 — What we are differentiating

By definition $v(p,m)=u\big(x(p,m)\big)$, where $x(p,m)$ solves

$$\max_{x}\;u(x)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad p\cdot x=m$$

So $v$ is the **value function** of the utility-maximisation problem: the maximum utility reachable, as a function of the parameters $p$ and $m$.

## Step 2 — Apply the envelope theorem

Form the Lagrangian:

$$\mathcal{L}=u(x)+\lambda\,(m-p\cdot x)$$

The envelope theorem says that the derivative of a value function with respect to a parameter equals the partial derivative of the Lagrangian with respect to that parameter, **evaluated at the optimum and holding the choice variables fixed**. The terms in $\partial x/\partial p_i$ vanish precisely because $x$ is already optimal — that is the content of the theorem, and it is the step worth naming.

Applying it twice:

$$\frac{\partial v}{\partial p_i}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial p_i}=-\lambda\,x_i,\qquad\qquad \frac{\partial v}{\partial m}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial m}=\lambda$$

## Step 3 — Divide out the multiplier

$$\frac{\partial v/\partial p_i}{\partial v/\partial m}=\frac{-\lambda x_i}{\lambda}=-x_i$$

$$\boxed{\;x_i(p,m)=-\,\frac{\partial v/\partial p_i}{\partial v/\partial m}\;}\qquad\blacksquare$$

## Step 4 — Why the sign comes out right

A rise in $p_i$ shrinks the budget set, so $\partial v/\partial p_i<0$. Local nonsatiation gives $\partial v/\partial m=\lambda>0$. The ratio is therefore negative, and the leading minus sign returns a **positive** quantity, as a demand must be.

Note also what $\lambda$ is: $\partial v/\partial m=\lambda$ says the multiplier is the **marginal utility of income**.

## Why it is useful

The identity reverses the direction of applied work. Instead of positing a utility function, solving the first-order conditions and hoping the resulting demand system can be estimated, the researcher specifies a flexible form for $v(p,m)$ directly and *differentiates* to obtain demands. That is how the indirect translog and the Almost Ideal Demand System are built.

The payoff is consistency for free: a system derived from a single $v$ automatically satisfies adding-up, homogeneity and Slutsky symmetry, instead of having those imposed as after-the-fact restrictions.

**Worked check.** For Cobb-Douglas, $v(p,m)=m\,a^{a}(1-a)^{1-a}p_1^{-a}p_2^{-(1-a)}$. Then $\partial v/\partial p_i=-\tfrac{a}{p_1}v$ and $\partial v/\partial m=v/m$, so the identity returns $x_1=am/p_1$ — the demand we already know.

> **The equation.** The total effect of a price change splits into a substitution effect and an income effect:
> $$\underbrace{\frac{\partial x_i(p,m)}{\partial p_j}}_{\text{total}}=\underbrace{\frac{\partial h_i(p,u)}{\partial p_j}}_{\text{substitution}}-\underbrace{x_j(p,m)\,\frac{\partial x_i(p,m)}{\partial m}}_{\text{income}}$$

![A fall in $p_1$: A to B is the substitution effect along the original indifference curve; B to C is the income effect.](content/figures/slutsky-decomposition.svg)

## What each term means

- **Total effect** — how observed demand actually moves when $p_j$ changes and income is held fixed. This is what we see in data.
- **Substitution effect** — the move *along the original indifference curve*. Relative prices have changed, so the consumer re-optimises even though real income is held constant by compensation.
- **Income effect** — the price change alters purchasing power. The size of that change is $x_j$, because losing $\Delta p_j$ on each of $x_j$ units costs $x_j\Delta p_j$ of real income.

## The proof

**Step 1 — Start from the duality identity.** At the utility level $u$ actually achieved, the compensated and uncompensated demands coincide:

$$h_i(p,u)=x_i\big(p,\,e(p,u)\big)$$

This holds *identically* in $p$ — it is true at every price vector, not just one. That is what licenses differentiating it.

**Step 2 — Differentiate both sides with respect to $p_j$.** The right-hand side has $p_j$ in two places: directly, and through $e(p,u)$. The chain rule gives

$$\frac{\partial h_i(p,u)}{\partial p_j}=\frac{\partial x_i(p,m)}{\partial p_j}+\frac{\partial x_i(p,m)}{\partial m}\cdot\frac{\partial e(p,u)}{\partial p_j}$$

**Step 3 — Apply Shephard's lemma.** The last derivative is just the compensated demand:

$$\frac{\partial e(p,u)}{\partial p_j}=h_j(p,u)=x_j(p,m)$$

the second equality holding because we evaluate at $m=e(p,u)$, where the two demands agree.

**Step 4 — Substitute and rearrange.**

$$\frac{\partial h_i}{\partial p_j}=\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_j}+x_j\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial m}\;\Longrightarrow\;\boxed{\;\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_j}=\frac{\partial h_i}{\partial p_j}-x_j\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial m}\;}$$

## Matrix form, two goods

Collecting all four cross-effects, with $D_px$ the matrix of price derivatives:

$$\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial p_1} & \dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial p_2}\\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial p_1} & \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial p_2}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{\partial h_1}{\partial p_1} & \dfrac{\partial h_1}{\partial p_2}\\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial h_2}{\partial p_1} & \dfrac{\partial h_2}{\partial p_2}\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}\dfrac{\partial x_1}{\partial m}\\[10pt] \dfrac{\partial x_2}{\partial m}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}x_1 & x_2\end{pmatrix}$$

compactly, $D_px = D_ph - (D_mx)\,x^{\mathsf T}$.

**The properties the matrix delivers** — this is the payoff, and where the marks are:

1. **The substitution matrix is symmetric**: $\partial h_i/\partial p_j=\partial h_j/\partial p_i$, because both equal $\partial^2 e/\partial p_i\partial p_j$ and the order of differentiation does not matter.
2. **It is negative semidefinite**, since $e$ is concave in prices. On the diagonal this gives $\partial h_i/\partial p_i\le 0$ — the **compensated own-price effect is never positive**. This is the only unambiguous sign in demand theory.
3. **The uncompensated effect has no guaranteed sign.** If good $i$ is inferior, $\partial x_i/\partial m<0$, so the income term is positive and can outweigh the substitution term. That is precisely the **Giffen** case, and the Slutsky equation shows it is the *only* way an upward-sloping demand curve can arise.

## Worked check on Cobb-Douglas

For $u=x_1^ax_2^{1-a}$ we have $x_1=am/p_1$, so $\partial x_1/\partial p_1=-am/p_1^2$. The decomposition splits it in the ratio $(1-a):a$ —

$$\underbrace{-\frac{(1-a)am}{p_1^{2}}}_{\text{substitution}}\;+\;\underbrace{\left(-\frac{a^{2}m}{p_1^{2}}\right)}_{\text{income}}=-\frac{am}{p_1^{2}}\;\checkmark$$

Both are negative, which is why Cobb-Douglas demand is always downward-sloping and a Cobb-Douglas good can never be Giffen.

questions.answer:
Demand theory does not merely say the consumer "chooses well". It says demand must satisfy **four properties**, and these are the whole observable content of the theory — anything satisfying them is consistent with utility maximisation, and anything violating them is not.

## 1. Homogeneous of degree zero in $(p,m)$

$$x_i(tp,\,tm)=x_i(p,m)\qquad\text{for all }t>0$$

**Why.** Scaling all prices and income by the same factor leaves the budget set $\{x:tp\cdot x\le tm\}$ literally unchanged, since $t$ cancels. The feasible set is the same, so the best point in it is the same.

**What it rules out — money illusion.** A consumer whose demand changed when every price and their income doubled would be responding to the *numbers* rather than to what they can actually buy. Only **relative** prices and **real** income matter.

## 2. Budget balance (adding-up)

$$\sum_i p_i\,x_i(p,m)=m$$

**Why.** Local nonsatiation. If any income were left unspent, there would be a strictly better bundle within reach, contradicting optimality. This is what licenses writing the constraint as an equality throughout.

Differentiating it gives two restrictions used constantly in applied work:

$$\sum_i p_i\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial m}=1,\qquad\qquad \sum_i p_i\frac{\partial x_i}{\partial p_j}+x_j=0$$

— the **Engel aggregation** and **Cournot aggregation** conditions.

## 3. The Slutsky matrix is symmetric

With $s_{ij}=\partial h_i/\partial p_j$ the compensated price effects,

$$s_{ij}=s_{ji}$$

**Why.** By Shephard's lemma $h_i=\partial e/\partial p_i$, so $s_{ij}=\partial^{2}e/\partial p_j\partial p_i$ — the Hessian of the expenditure function. Young's theorem makes the order of differentiation irrelevant.

**What it says.** The compensated effect of good $j$'s price on good $i$ equals the effect of good $i$'s price on good $j$. It is a genuinely testable restriction, and it is not obvious — nothing in casual intuition requires it.

## 4. The Slutsky matrix is negative semidefinite

$$z^{\mathsf T}S\,z\le0\qquad\text{for every }z$$

**Why.** $e(p,u)$ is **concave in prices**, and a concave function has a negative semidefinite Hessian.

**What it contains.** Take $z$ as the $i$-th unit vector: $s_{ii}\le0$, so the **compensated own-price effect is never positive**. This is the law of demand in its only exact form — it holds for Hicksian demand always, and for Marshallian demand except when a strong inferior-good income effect intervenes, which is the Giffen case.

## Why the four together are the point

They are the **integrability conditions**. A demand system that is homogeneous of degree zero, satisfies the budget identity, and has a symmetric negative semidefinite Slutsky matrix can be *generated* by some well-behaved preference ordering — and that ordering can be recovered.

So the four properties are not a checklist bolted onto the theory. They are exactly what utility maximisation implies about behaviour, and exactly what behaviour must show for utility maximisation to be a possible explanation of it. That is why an econometrician imposes them, and why finding one violated is evidence against the model rather than against the data.
